summary_html: A **parent/guardian/child requests help** without a substantiated allegation. FFPSA created a federal pathway for **prevention services** to avert removal and stabilize families before a case escalates.
authority_html: - **Family First Prevention Services Act (2018)** — prevention services, kinship support; shifts upstream from removal to support

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Weaver v. Roanoke Department of Human Resources
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed the termination of both parents' residual parental rights because the record contained no evidence that social agencies made the 'reasonable and appropriate efforts' that Code § 16.1-283(C)(2) requires before rights may be severed, and directed that termination statutes be read to preserve the parent-child relationship where possible.
key_cases.relevance: Virginia's foundational termination case arises from children placed in foster care partly at the parents' own request, and holds that the agency, not the family, bears the burden of showing services were offered.
key_cases.quote: Statutes terminating the legal relationship between parent and child should be interpreted consistently with the governmental objective of preserving, when possible, the parent-child relationship.

key_cases.case_name: Toombs v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(C)(2), holding that whether parental visitation must continue after a termination petition is filed is decided case by case with the child's best interests as the guiding principle, and that clear and convincing evidence supported the statutory factors here.
key_cases.relevance: The children entered foster care through the parents' own approach to the agency, and the Court still required the Division to prove the statutory grounds by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: The question must be resolved, however, in light of the facts of each case, with the best interests of the child as the guiding principle.

key_cases.case_name: Harris v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination as to the mother but reversed as to the father, holding that undisputed evidence that a parent was never offered or provided services overcomes the statutory prima facie case and puts the agency to full proof of the § 16.1-283(C)(2) factors.
key_cases.relevance: A parent who never asked for and was never offered help cannot be terminated on a prima facie showing alone.
key_cases.quote: where, as here, there is undisputed evidence that a parent has not been offered or provided services, the prima facie case is overcome

key_cases.case_name: Rocka v. Roanoke County Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed an order granting a welfare board permanent custody with the right to place for adoption, holding that in a contest between a parent and a non-parent the rule of comparative best interests does not apply and the board must prove parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence, and directing an interlocutory award of custody to the mother so she could demonstrate her present fitness.
key_cases.relevance: The mother herself asked the Board to take her children and place them in foster care until she could find work and a home, and the Court held that request could not be converted into permanent severance without proof of unfitness.
key_cases.quote: We believe that the evidence of parental unfitness in this record is less than clear and convincing and, thus, insufficient to divest a parent of custody of its child.

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed the denial of a mother's petition to regain custody, holding that because a prior juvenile court order entered after her voluntary relinquishment, an investigation and a hearing had altered her custody rights she bore the burden of showing changed circumstances, but reversed the interlocutory adoption decree because the prospective adoptive parents were separating.
key_cases.relevance: The mother's own voluntary written relinquishment of custody, acted on after a thorough investigation and a hearing, is what shifted the burden against her when she later asked for her child back.
key_cases.quote: the burden was not upon the Shepards, as the mother argues, to show parental unfitness

mandatory_reporters: Designated professionals only — Virginia is NOT a universal-reporter state (Va. Code § 63.2-1509(A))
Any person licensed to practice medicine or any of the healing arts
Any hospital resident or intern, and any person employed in the nursing profession
Any person employed as a social worker or family-services specialist
Any probation officer
Any teacher or other person employed in a public or private school, kindergarten, or child day program (§ 22.1-289.02)
Any person providing full-time or part-time child care for pay on a regularly planned basis
Any mental health professional
Any law-enforcement officer or animal control officer
Any mediator eligible to receive court referrals (§ 8.01-576.8)
Any professional staff person employed by a private or state-operated hospital, institution, or facility to which children have been committed or placed for care and treatment
Any person 18 or older associated with or employed by any public or private organization responsible for the care, custody, or control of children
Any court-appointed special advocate (CASA) designated under § 9.1-151 et seq.
Any person 18 or older who has received Department of Social Services-approved training in recognizing and reporting child abuse and neglect
Any local department employee who determines eligibility for public assistance
Any emergency medical services provider certified by the Board of Health (§ 32.1-111.5)
Any athletic coach, director, or other person 18 or older employed by or volunteering with a public or private sports organization or team, or a school athletics program
Administrators or employees 18 or older of public or private day camps, youth centers, and youth recreation programs
Any person employed by a public or private institution of higher education, other than an attorney providing legal representation to a client
Any minister, priest, rabbi, imam, or duly accredited practitioner of a religious organization, subject to the clergy-privilege exceptions in § 63.2-1509(A)(19)
Any person who engages in the practice of behavior analysis (§ 54.1-2900)

timeline_requirements.deadline: Face-to-face contact within the response time set at intake; within 24 hours if the child is under 2
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Worker must document in writing why the contact or observation was not made (22VAC40-705-80)

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (extendable to a total of 60 days on written justification, or to 90 days in a joint law-enforcement investigation)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute sets no penalty; any extension requires written justification and the local department must notify the alleged abuser or neglector and the child's parents (Va. Code § 63.2-1505(B)(5); 22VAC40-705-120)
